objective: Configure PolicyExceptions: exempting specific resources from specific rules, scoping and approving exceptions
secondaryObjectives: Policy reports: PolicyReport and ClusterPolicyReport resources, result statuses (pass, fail, warn, error, skip) and reading them with kubectl

sources.cite: CNCF, Kyverno Certified Associate (KCA) certification page
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the certification body's page, found by WebSearch. Confirms the exam domains and weights: Fundamentals of Kyverno 18%, Installation, Configuration, and Upgrades 18%, Kyverno CLI 12%, Applying Policies 10%, Writing Policies 32%, Policy Management 10%. The objective wording is the course seed's.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: a PolicyException names the policy and rule names it applies to and uses match and exclude to select resources; its creation should be controlled so it is authorized; exceptions turn report results from fail to skip.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: exceptions are disabled by default, and enabling them requires setting exceptionNamespace to say which namespaces they may be used in; a skip result records the applied exception.

The company, the clusters, the policies and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You run policy governance at Kestrel Mutual, a fictional insurer. The disallow-host-path policy is enforced cluster-wide. A legacy document-scanning app in the scan namespace needs one hostPath mount to reach a scanner driver until it is replaced next quarter.
handover: The policy: disallow-host-path, rule host-path, Enforce, all namespaces except kube-system.
PolicyExceptions are enabled; today anyone with edit can create one in any namespace.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

choices.label: Switch disallow-host-path to Audit cluster-wide until the app is replaced

whoPrompt.title: Anyone can exempt themselves
whoPrompt.context: Exceptions can be created in any namespace by any developer.

choices.label: Configure Kyverno to accept exceptions only from a policy-exceptions namespace, and give create rights there only to the security team, through a reviewed pull request

effects.log: Exceptions live in one namespace that only security can write.

choices.feedback: Restricting where exceptions are accepted and who can write them turns exceptions into approvals.

choices.label: Keep the permissions and review new exceptions weekly

choices.label: Leave it: teams are trusted
choices.feedback: Any policy can be bypassed by anyone who can write an exception.

effects.log: Skips are watched; the date is tracked.

choices.feedback: A skip result shows the exception being used; anything else skipped means the scope is wrong.

choices.label: Put a calendar reminder for next quarter
choices.feedback: You will remember to remove it, but not notice if it starts covering more than it should.

choices.label: Nothing more: the exception is in Git

scoring.modelReasoning: A PolicyException exempts named resources from named rules of a named policy, so it can be as narrow as one Deployment and one rule; excluding a namespace in the policy or switching to Audit removes protection from everything else. Because an exception bypasses policy, Kyverno should accept exceptions only from a namespace that only approvers can write. PolicyReports show skip results where an exception applies, which is how you see it being used and notice when it covers more than intended.
